message.content:
the clickup connector check that if u need heres our task from clickup i pasted too its the corpus index from datalab Sir's words: on big projects the files get way too much to feed into an agent, it skips stuff and doesn't link connections. Reliably pulling up facts becomes a bottleneck as it misses more and more detail the further it goes. This has happened to him 4 or 5 times, and it's happening right now on the Pakistan auto policy work. He's already tried the straightforward agentic approach and many rounds of prompt engineering, and hit the same wall both times, so assume prompting is not the answer. This isn't "use an agent," it's building the layer that makes an agent survive a large corpus.

The end state is this: point it at any folder on his drive — hundreds of folders, thousands of files, no pre-organisation, a layout nobody has seen before. He asks something vague and niche, like how Pakistan's X trajectory looks. The agent goes straight to the exact material wherever it's buried, pulls from several sources at once, and answers. Portable, so the same thing works on any repo, his or mine. Every recommendation gets judged against whether it gets us there.

His actual workflow is a hard constraint on all of it. He cds into the big folder, runs Claude Code in the terminal, and works. So whatever we build has to live inside Claude Code — no separate app, no server he starts by hand, no UI. Anything that needs a step he has to remember is dead, because he won't do it and neither will I after week two. Index refresh can't be manual either; it has to fire on session start or on change, because a stale index is worse than no index, it silently points at files that moved. The harder part is that Claude Code reaches for its own glob and grep first, so an index sitting there unused solves nothing — the system either has to replace those paths or be unmistakably the front door, and that's a design problem rather than a config detail. One good side effect of the CLI setup is that measurement comes nearly free, since Claude Code writes session transcripts containing tool calls and hooks fire on tool use, so reading back which files the agent actually opened doesn't need custom instrumentation.

Worth telling him plainly: some meaningful share of what he's been fighting with prompts is a filed bug in his exact tool. Claude Code issue #16043 — Glob's ripgrep hits a timeout on a large directory, gets SIGTERM'd, and returns "0 results" silently instead of erroring, so the agent believes nothing is there. Plus Read-tool silent truncation at 2000 lines, where the model reasons over the head of a file as if it were the whole thing, and #12534 for subdirectory contents going invisible in large repos. NOTE: this framing is now partly wrong — see the round-two review section at the bottom. #12534 is the VS Code extension and not his setup, #16043 is closed as a duplicate, and the Read claim doesn't hold in the form written here. Nothing from this paragraph goes in front of sir as written.

Still undecided: whether this ships as an MCP server, a skill, hooks, or just CLAUDE.md plus scripts. All four are viable, they fail differently, and that choice probably determines the whole shape of the build, so it should be settled before anything gets written. Both round-two reports have a strong view on this — see below — but it hasn't been tested on our own setup yet.

One thing the earlier framing got wrong is granularity. File-level retrieval isn't the finish line, because "Pakistan's X trajectory" is answered by one table on page 340 of a 600-page Economic Survey, not by a file — finding the right PDF still leaves 600 pages that won't fit in context. So there are two nested retrieval problems, which document and then where inside it. Trajectory questions make it worse, since the same series across ten years lives in ten different fat PDFs formatted differently each year, and the system has to know they're the same series. That's the hardest question class and also the most realistic for what he does.

On coverage, "98% scanned" was covering two different requirements. At index time full coverage is achievable and checkable — every file walked, indexed, hashed, and coverage becomes a number you can print, like 47,203 of 48,100 indexed with the 897 failures listed and explained as corrupt, encrypted, image-only or permission-denied. That turns silent misses into a visible exception list. At query time you want the opposite, deliberately tiny, because reading everything per question is the context rot we're trying to escape — read five files, but with provable grounds that the rest were ruled out by something that saw them. The honest framing for sir is that "the agent looked at everything" is a promise no system can keep, while "everything is in the index and here are the 897 exceptions" is one we can actually hand him.

What the build has to work out: what the index knows about the corpus without loading it, and how that works on an arbitrary tree with no prior structure. Page and table level addressing inside fat PDFs rather than just file paths. A retrieval policy that's explainable, since a silent omission is the exact failure mode. Some answer for what happens when the relevant set still exceeds the window — ranking, summarisation, staged retrieval. Omission reporting, so the agent states what it didn't look at, because degrading silently is what makes the current setup untrustworthy. A specific test that relationships between documents survive retrieval, since dropping links is half of what he reported. And portability, meaning one command against any directory with config living inside the target folder so each repo carries its own index.

Test tree — ra-ship copy

Testing runs on a local Desktop copy of the ra-ship workspace, so nothing there is precious. Real numbers from DOCUMENTATION_RECON.md: 17.85 GiB, 217,517 files, 94 tracked on GitHub.

File count needs splitting before it means anything. The bulk is ABS_PES_PBS_Extraction_Test/02_tool_runs/ at 6.33 GiB of venvs and model caches, roughly 175k of the 217k. Actual documents are around 42k: Source Documents Organized (933, 900 PDFs), pbs-corpus raw (355, SHA-256 validated), extraction outputs (1,073), Arsalan Archive (37,928), Budget EDA (929), the read-only mirror (651).

The venv question is not a speed question. Even if the index excludes them, Claude Code's own Glob and Grep still walk them, and an agent that opens twenty site-packages files before reaching a fiscal PDF has burned its window — same context rot, sourced from libraries instead of old teaching material. Which means exclusion probably has to be enforced at the tool level rather than the index level, and that lands straight back on the undecided front-door / delivery-mechanism problem. Worth noting the index still has to account for them as intentionally_excluded:venv rather than letting 175k files vanish from the coverage number.

What this tree gives for free that the generator would have had to fake. Real duplicates with no canonical marker — 02_Source_Documents_Read_Only/ is an explicit 651-file mirror, PES Archive Copy duplicates Pakistan Economic Surveys, and Archive.zip (876.7 MB) plus Budget EDA.zip (825.1 MB) hold copies of folders that also exist uncompressed. Real same-series-across-years, which is the hardest open question — ABS FY2017-18 to 2026-27, Annual Budget Statements FY2010-11 to FY2026-27, subcodes_long.csv spanning FY2010-11 to 2025-26, split across three unrelated branches. Real fat PDFs for sub-document addressing — Economic_Survey_2025-26.pdf at 376 pages / 56.1 MB, DFG multi-volume demands, chapter-level PES splits. Real markdown drift including a SOURCE_SELECTION.md sitting there marked BLOCKED. And with 94 of 217k files tracked, gitignored is the default state rather than an edge case, so the tracked/ignored contrast has to come from 00_Workspace_Guide/ or 04_Research_Outputs/Deliverables/.

What it can't give: recall scoring. Canaries work because you plant the string yourself. "Did it find all 12 files mentioning X" needs ground truth nobody has for this tree. That's what the generated corpus is for — this replaces the canary suite's synthetic tree, not the generator.

Canary suite — pass 1 spec

A canary is a unique nonsense string planted in a file so a later lookup is unambiguous — no false positives possible, either it found it or it didn't. Pass 1 goes into the existing ra-ship copy. Pass 2 goes into the generated corpus once it exists, since that tree will wrap this one and change shape. Revisions to pass 1 are rev numbers, not new passes — don't call a re-plant "pass 2" or it collides with the generated-corpus set later.

12-15 phrases, one per location, never reused so a failure identifies the exact case. Phrases must not share a common token — a shared prefix means one grep finds the whole set and everything passes for the wrong reason. They also shouldn't share a common shape, since a uniform word-8hex-6digits pattern is one regex away from being the same leak; vary the forms, or record the shared shape in the companion md so a suspiciously clean result can be read correctly. Grep the tree for each before planting to confirm zero hits — won't reach inside the two big zips, accepted since the strings are random.

Coverage priority when combinations exceed phrases: format, then depth, then tracked vs ignored, then branch spread. Output a coverage matrix showing which combinations got one and which didn't. If a canary gets removed for a naming or placement problem, the case it was carrying has to be re-planted somewhere else — dropping the file drops the case.

Format — PDF, CSV, markdown, .html, .docx if python-docx is available. Check pypdf and python-docx importability first and skip rather than improvise. At least one canary must sit deep inside a genuinely fat PDF (200+ pages), since a created one-pager tests nothing about page-level addressing.
Depth — repo top level, ~4 deep, and the real maximum, measured excluding 02_tool_runs since site-packages nesting gives a meaningless number. The top-level case matters on its own since it's the one an agent should never miss.
Tracked vs ignored — at least one in 00_Workspace_Guide or 04_Research_Outputs/Deliverables.
Branches — Source Documents Organized, Arsalan Archive, Budget EDA, pbs-corpus, read-only mirror. One in a hidden dot-prefixed dir if one exists.
One inside 02_tool_runs — the question is whether an ignore rule for that directory turns out overbroad and swallows things outside it. Exactly one, and nothing else load-bearing in there, since a venv exclusion rule will remove whatever sits inside.

Do not inject into hash-validated or schema-dependent files: anything under Source Documents Organized/Provenance/, sources.csv, manifest.csv, fetch_log.jsonl, the per-year manifests in Budget EDA, subcodes_long.csv, subcodes_wide_enriched.csv. This applies to PDFs too, not just CSVs — before injecting into any source PDF, grep the Budget EDA per-year manifests and the provenance files for that filename, since a checksummed document that stops matching its manifest is a broken validation rather than a planted string. If unsure whether a file is load-bearing, create a new one instead. Injection is fine in markdown, .html, loose text, throwaway CSVs.

Two traps that would invalidate the results. Created files must match their surroundings — same extension as neighbours, plausible naming and size, and nothing in the filename that names the experiment, or the file gets found for being the odd one out and proves nothing about depth. Timestamps must be restored, since every touched file otherwise carries today's mtime in a tree where everything else is months or years old, and any recency ranking surfaces exactly the canaries. Record original mtime, restore after editing, set created files to match neighbours.

Manifest lives at C:\Users\ali\Desktop\canary_manifest_pass1.csv****, never inside the repo — an answer key sitting in the tree gets found by the agent searching for canaries and everything passes for the wrong reason. Columns: phrase, absolute path, cases covered, injected or created, backup path, original mtime, restored mtime, blank pass/fail. Originals backed up to C:\Users\ali\Desktop\canary_backups_pass1\ before editing, path recorded, so reversal is restore-from-copy rather than a described diff. Companion markdown alongside explaining what it is, when planted, what the cases mean, how to reverse.

Nothing gets committed or pushed.

Running it. Since the workflow is terminal Claude Code, the test isn't "does my indexer find the phrase," it's "does Claude Code find it when asked." Run as a real session in the ra-ship copy and read the transcript for which files it actually opened. Baseline first with no index at all — that number is what says how bad Glob/Grep already are on a 217k tree, and it's what justifies building anything. Before any baseline run, confirm the previous revision rolled back clean — git status plus a grep for the retired phrases — since a leftover string from an earlier revision contaminates the numbers.

Scale calibration — sir's real tree

Sir's tree is around 100 folders max and 10k files as a hard ceiling. Denser and smaller than the earlier spec assumed.

Size ladder is 500 / 2k / 5k / 15k, down from 500 / 2k / 10k / 50k. 15k is one rung above his real maximum so there's proven margin without spending generation time on a scale that will never be hit. Ladder should be a config parameter rather than four hardcoded sizes.

Folder counts fall out of the shape rules — depth 2 to 7, folders ranging empty to 400 files, no relationship between name and contents. Rough working figures: ~30 folders at 500 files, ~100 at 2k, ~250 at 5k, ~600 at 15k. Arithmetic off the constraints, not spec'd.

Tree shape mostly shallow and wide with a handful of deep branches. At ~100 folders you can't branch much at depth 7 without spending the whole folder budget on a few chains.

This shifts what the harness tests. With few, fat folders, "which folder" is nearly free — the hard part is which of the 400 files inside, then which page inside that file. Lines up with sub-document addressing being the real problem. Weight toward fat PDFs and dense folders, away from deep nesting, and the fat PDFs need to genuinely hit 200-800 pages or the test won't bite at page level.

Open: sir's actual format breakdown is unknown. The mix below is the spec's assumption. Worth a quick count on his tree before generating.

None of that is measurable without a corpus we control, so the test harness gets built first. A seeded, reproducible generator script that emits a tree plus an answer key. What it's simulating is an econ professor's drive — fifteen years of accumulated material with an eighteen-month agent-era layer sitting on top. Era strata, abandoned reorganisation attempts, teaching material repeating by year, co-author folders where someone else's naming convention took over. The bulk of it is inherited and passive, papers downloaded once and never opened again, with the active work as a thin recent layer, and an agent that can't tell those apart burns its whole window on 2011.

Format mix runs to PDFs at 60-70% of file count with many genuinely fat at 200-800 pages, CSVs around 15%, markdown 10-15% spread at every depth and thinning out as you go back in time, JSON and agent files at a few percent clustered in the recent layer, then a tail of .dta, .do, .R, .xlsx, .docx and .zip. At the 15k top rung that's roughly 9-10.5k PDFs, ~2.2k CSVs, ~1.5-2.2k markdown, a few hundred JSON and agent files, and 500-800 in the tail. Given the density point above, push the fat-PDF share up within that band. The CSVs should be what an econ prof actually has rather than synthetic filler — WDI and World Bank pulls, IMF WEO, PBS and SBP series, survey microdata extracts, regression output tables, an RA-cleaned dataset sitting next to its raw version, Stata exports beside the .dta, journal replication package data, a co-author's dataset with their column naming, panel country-year data, SBP EasyData scrapes, PhD-era leftovers, teaching problem-set data. Generic synthetic CSVs won't produce the near-miss confusion the test needs.

What makes it chaotic rather than just big: naming conventions that differ by era and sometimes within a single folder, depth varying unpredictably with the same kind of file appearing shallow and deep, folders ranging from empty to 400 files with no relationship between the name and the contents, formats mixed within directories rather than sorted, duplicates scattered across unrelated branches with nothing marking which is canonical, zips containing copies of folders that also exist uncompressed, and a few genuinely unreadable files.

The markdown sediment is its own layer and probably the worst one for retrieval, because stale docs look authoritative. A README, a PLAN.md, a NOTES.md — the agent reads it and treats it as a description of reality, when half of them describe a state that stopped existing months ago. This matters more on a dense tree, since with fewer folders the stale README at the top of a fat folder is what the agent hits first and trusts. So the corpus needs readmes at every depth with some current and some describing a folder that got restructured under them, plans that stop mid-way, handoff notes from people who left, contradicting AGENT.md and CLAUDE.md files at multiple levels, and docs an agent generated once and nobody updated. Nothing in the file says which is which; same extension, same headers, and sometimes the stale one is better written because whoever wrote it had time and whoever abandoned the replacement didn't. Seed this layer from the real ra-ship docs, since that gives real drift with verifiable ground truth, then bury it in generated sediment. Telling finished-and-true from abandoned-and-stale is a distinct test from "can it find the file" and probably needs a different answer.

Build order for the generator is skeleton first, deterministic from the seed and empty. Then plant the answers before any filler, writing the key as you go, because planting last means searching your own corpus to find where things ended up. Then distractors derived mechanically from the answer files and placed in different branches. Then bulk filler to hit the target count. The first three passes stay fixed across sizes and only the filler scales. Script owns volume and structure; the LLM writes 20-30 genuinely distinct human-voiced docs once and the script mutates and recombines those at volume, so no LLM call per file. Model choice doesn't matter here since the corpus is disposable — save the budget for the system being tested. Have the generator plant pass-2 canaries itself as part of the run rather than as a separate step after, since it's already writing an answer key and that keeps them deterministic from the seed.

The properties that make it a test rather than just a big folder are worth being deliberate about. A size ladder, same answer key at 500, 2k, 5k and 15k files, so the output is a degradation curve rather than pass/fail and we learn where it breaks instead of just that it does. Retrieval logged separately from answers, so an agent that opened 40 wrong files and guessed right doesn't score the same as one that went straight to three — the silent-miss failure is only visible in recall, and that's also how the subagent question gets measured, whether they covered different branches or all piled into one. Distractor density of 10-20 near-misses around every planted answer that match the query better lexically but are wrong: older versions, perturbed values, drafts on the same topic, co-author copies. Without those the corpus is merely big and proves nothing. Multi-branch questions that can't be answered from any single branch, which are the ones that produce plausible wrong answers when only part gets read. Absence questions where the correct answer is that it isn't in the corpus, which catches invention and matters most given his report is about what's missing from the data. Name and content mismatch, files whose names tell you nothing like SRO_1247.pdf or scan0043.pdf and files whose names lie like final_data.csv holding the superseded version, forcing content indexing over path matching. And regenerable by seed, so changing the seed and rerunning shows whether the numbers hold or whether we overfit to one arrangement.

After the harness, run it against the Pakistan auto policy project, since that's the live instance of the failure. Success is that it either surfaces the right material or explicitly says what it skipped.

Sir's stated priority order is documentation first with nothing moving until it passes, then crawlers, then Supabase, then checking in with Arslan, so this queues behind that. Though documentation and this task may turn out to be the same work — if the corpus catalogue deliverable is generated rather than hand-written, meaning a script walks the tree, hashes every file and emits the markdown, then it's simultaneously the documentation he's waiting on and the index the agent queries instead of walking folders, and it stays true because it's regenerated rather than maintained. Worth checking whether the existing SOURCE_CORPUS_CATALOGUE.md is generated or typed.

This overlaps with Research ontologies (86eyuderj) and Rulebook of relations between datasets (86eyuderv), since the archivist needs the rulebook to bridge a vague concept like "X trajectory" to specific series and tables. One thing to keep in mind there is that definitions aren't relations — a metric layer stops the five-different-series problem but doesn't encode something like GNI and GDP diverging through factor income abroad, so if you're claiming one you should check the other. That gap is still open. Deterministic checks layer (86eyuderp) is a separate workstream but sits downstream of the same rulebook.

Research review — round one, both reports read against this spec

Two deep research passes are now in and both have been reviewed: the Claude one and an earlier GPT one. Neither saw this spec, so where they independently land on something written here, that's corroboration rather than echo.

Settled, stop researching these. Extraction tooling: Docling vs MinerU vs Marker, with Marker ruled out on licensing (GPL-3.0 code plus a RAIL-M weight licence restricting commercial use above a revenue threshold). Vector store options: LEANN, LanceDB, Chroma, Qdrant, SQLite FTS5. GraphRAG is priced out — roughly $33k to index a single 5GB dataset, and Microsoft's own LazyGraphRAG framing puts full GraphRAG at 1000x the indexing cost of vector RAG. Buy-not-build document layers exist and are documented: paperless-ngx, DEVONthink, ICIJ Datashare, OCCRP Aleph.

Corroborated across passes. Coverage accounting arrived at independently by the GPT report, with a usable schema: a per-file status enum of indexed_ok / unsupported_type / parse_failed:reason / intentionally_excluded:reason / pending, and never an unknown, surfaced through an index_health() call. That closes most of the coverage question above. Hierarchical retrieval — document summary, then sections/pages, then fine-grained chunks — is a partial answer to the sub-document problem. Both reports independently say do not split subagents by directory branch, though they disagree on what to split by instead (retrieval strategy vs concept) and neither has evidence, so treat that as a hypothesis to test.

New named things worth acting on. ripgrep-all (rga) greps inside PDFs and Office docs by shelling out to pdftotext/pandoc. Recoll, a Xapian full-text indexer documented at 11M+ documents, which the Claude pass had listed as an empty search; its trap is directly relevant, in that it remembers files that failed extraction and will not retry them until you run recollindex -k, so it silently carries holes forever. LlamaParse Index + MCP, whose tools are findFilesInIndex / grepFileFromIndex / readFileFromIndex / retrieveFromIndex, Starter around $50/month.

Still open after round one. Same-series-across-years. Delivery mechanism, with both reports simply assuming MCP without comparing it to hooks, a skill, or CLAUDE.md plus scripts, and neither addressing getting in front of Claude Code's built-in Glob and Grep. Query-time omission reporting. No existing benchmark for retrieval over messy real-world file trees.

One contradiction to settle. The round-one Claude report says index staleness is unlikely to matter because sources rarely change. That's wrong for the reason stated at the top of this task: it isn't the source PDFs changing, it's the working tree churning around them, and a stale index pointing at a moved path is worse than no index.

Research review — round two, two more reports

Round two is in: a Claude report and a GPT report, both run against the six-point round-two prompt. Neither saw the other. Recording what they say; none of it is tested on our own setup yet.

Bug verification — #16043 checked directly, not just reported. The issue is real, opened Jan 2 on version 2.0.76, repro exactly as described: Glob invokes ripgrep with --no-ignore --hidden, a 107GB gitignored ActiveStorage directory blows the ~10s timeout, Claude Code sends SIGTERM, debug log shows rg error (signal=SIGTERM, code=null, stderr: ), 0 results, and the same command run manually completes in 10.5s and finds the file. But it was closed as a duplicate of #4486 on Jan 5, auto-closed by a bot after a 3-day window with the bug, has repro and area:tools labels stripped, then auto-locked Jan 14. No human review, no fix version. So closed does not mean fixed, and the ticket to actually cite is #4486 (status not yet checked). The GPT report had this right; the round-two Claude report said the issue was open, which is wrong.

#12534 — both round-two reports independently say it's the VS Code extension, titled "VS Code Extension cannot detect files in subdirectories of large codebases," and the reporter explicitly says the terminal CLI saw all files including subdirectories fine. So it does not describe sir's setup and the framing at the top of this task is wrong. Also closed as duplicate. GPT names #43587 (Linux TUI file picker) as the nearer analogue for a terminal user.

#42542 — both confirm real and open, tagged area:core / bug / has repro. GPT gives the reporter's own boundary: affected on 2.1.90, last good version 2.1.81, regression appearing around 2.1.89/2.1.90 — the reporter's observation, not an Anthropic postmortem. Also that DISABLE_AUTO_COMPACT=true does not stop the microcompactions while DISABLE_COMPACT=true does but kills manual /compact too. The Claude report could not pin the version string at all and attributes the change to a silent server-side GrowthBook flag, citing a leaked-source analysis and an Anthropic Apr 23 postmortem admitting context-management bugs, plus feature request #7176.

Read 2000-line truncation — still not reconciled, four passes in. Claude report cites #6910 and #28783. GPT cites #6910, #22699 and #20223, and says a filed bug matching "Read always silently truncates at 2000 lines" does not exist in that form: the 2000-line default is documented behaviour, #6910 reports the opposite failure (ignoring the limit and blowing the token ceiling, closed as not planned), and #20223 is the one documenting genuine silent truncation, specifically through the @ attachment mechanism on both CLI and VS Code. Still non-overlapping issue numbers between sources.

Extra issues named this round. #15248 (one permission-denied subdirectory kills the whole Glob, returns 0 results), #27171 (intermittent empty results on small directories with no timeout involved), #63525 (built-in Grep/Glob unavailable under ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=1), #33106 (PreToolUse permissionDecision:"deny" is not enforced for MCP tool calls — hook fires, returns deny, MCP tool runs anyway), #22699 (a working third-party smart-read PreToolUse hook that intercepts Read, denies oversized reads and redirects the model — proven precedent for the enforcement pattern).

Delivery mechanism — both reports land in the same place independently. MCP server holds the retrieval capability, a PreToolUse hook is the enforcement layer, SessionStart handles refresh, permissions / --disallowedTools are the hard lever, and CLAUDE.md drops to ten lines of policy with no execution power. Neither found any supported mechanism that transparently substitutes an MCP call inside an attempted built-in Glob/Grep invocation — deny-and-redirect is the only available route. Because of #33106 the deny has to point at the built-ins and let the model fall through to MCP, not the reverse. Deny rules also don't cover rg/grep/find run through Bash, so those need denying separately, and the docs hedge that Read deny rules apply to Grep/Glob/LS on a best-effort basis only. GPT's refinement is to deny broad corpus crawls conditionally rather than globally, since Glob and Grep are still wanted when Claude is editing scripts. Working precedents named: Beacon (MIT, closest template, PreToolUse deny with additionalContext redirect, PostToolUse re-embed, PreCompact status re-injection), ContextStream (blocks Glob/Grep/Search/Explore/Task but only when the project is indexed, graceful fallthrough), ck-search, grepai, and the #22699 smart-read hook. Overly broad PreToolUse matchers measured at ~80ms/call, so match only Grep|Glob. PreToolUse fires before the permission check so a deny holds even under --dangerously-skip-permissions, but it does not fire for @-referenced files. None of this has been tested on our own setup — that's the next thing to run.

Staleness — both round-two reports side against round one. Path is the wrong primary key; identity should be a content hash (BLAKE3 or SHA-256) with path demoted to a mutable alias, same model as git-annex, DataLad and IPFS CIDs. GPT pushes it further into an address format — research://sha256/<content-id>/page/340/table/4.2, resolved to a current path at read time — and flags storing PDF page index and printed page label separately, since government reports have covers and roman-numeral front matter and the two never match. Claude report's refresh design: SessionStart does an incremental reconcile rather than a full reindex, fast-hash by size and mtime first, BLAKE3 only on suspects, new hash means index, known hash at a new path means just update the path, missing hash becomes a coverage-report entry rather than a silent miss.

Sub-document addressing — the two reports go different routes. Claude report names pdf-mcp (jztan, MIT, pip install pdf-mcp) as an off-the-shelf starting point: hybrid BM25 + semantic with RRF across a folder, document and page provenance, tables and images each returned with bbox and clip coordinates, corpus warm/overview/search tools, SQLite cache, Tesseract OCR, hidden-text flagging; 94 stars and 1 watcher though, so fork-target not dependency. Underneath it: Docling HybridChunker and HierarchicalChunker with every element carrying prov (page_no + bbox), with the docling-serve #613 gotcha that the HTTP chunk endpoint returns unresolved JSON pointers so bbox and page go missing inline; pdfplumber for known regions; Camelot with a per-table accuracy score you can threshold on, text-based PDFs only; Table Transformer for harder layouts; DuckDB over extracted CSVs as the numeric layer; RFC 8118 #page= fragments and W3C TextQuoteSelector as citation formats. GPT report goes visual instead: Sentence Transformers v6 MultiVectorEncoder with ColQwen2.5 for page-image retrieval, so relevance can come from table layout rather than extracted prose (note colpali-engine is deprecated for new deployments), plus PageIndex's local SDK for building a hierarchical section tree inside one long document, plus Unstructured's chunk-by-title model as a pattern worth copying even without its extractor. Neither report costs out running deep extraction across a whole tree, which is the obvious constraint here — open.

Same-series across years — both confirm nothing off the shelf exists. Claude report's three gaps: no open-source Pakistan harmoniser (only one-shot census digitisations, cerp-analytics/pbs2017 and colincookman/pakistan_census), no vintage/point-in-time library outside FRED/ALFRED, and WB/IMF SDMX doesn't carry province-level yearbook tables. Its answer is a crosswalk.yaml keyed by canonical series ID with vintages keyed by content hash carrying page/table/bbox/column map/rebasing notes, sdmx1 (v2.27.0, Aug 2026) for anything WB/IMF publish and explicitly not the dead pandaSDMX, MetricFlow (Apache-2.0 since Oct 2025) or Cube if he wants declared metrics, and Splink or dedupe for column matching while admitting both are row-level entity resolution and therefore awkward for the actual question. GPT report frames it as entity resolution and goes further: a canonical series registry as SQL (series + series_alias with match_method, match_score, review_status, reviewed_by), Valentine as the schema-matching candidate generator since it's purpose-built for finding relationships between columns across tabular datasets, pyJedAI once a series is normalised into a record, OpenRefine for the ambiguous review queue. Its two useful specifics: government tables put series in rows not columns, so normalise each candidate into a record (label, table title, agency, unit, frequency, geography, dimensions, first/last period, values) and match those instead of raw table schemas; and numeric overlap is strong identity evidence — if the 2022 report reprints the 2018-2020 observations under a changed row label and the values match, that's evidence of one series. Neither can automate base-year rebasing or chain-linking splices; both say record the break rather than force the merge. Both flag SBP EasyData's metadata API (announced Feb 2025) as worth mining before parsing SBP PDFs, and neither found a PBS SDMX or statistical API.

Coverage accounting. Claude report names Apache Tika's tika-eval as the one real off-the-shelf option — H2/SQLite output, exception-by-mime and full exception-detail reports, run by Tika itself against ~3M files, docs warn it won't scale to hundreds of millions. GPT names Tika Pipes for the same role as a broad file-health probe. Both then say the hand-rolled version is better because you control the taxonomy: walk, hash, attempt-parse with a timeout, classify into a fixed enum (corrupt / encrypted / password_protected / image_only_needs_ocr / permission_denied / unsupported_format / too_large / timeout), record (path, hash, size, mtime, status, error_class, error_msg, attempted_at) to SQLite, report by GROUP BY. BLAKE3 or xxhash for speed. Both note it doubles as the content-hash index foundation.

Omission reporting — both say the strong version is impossible. Top-k means "ranked highest by this procedure," not "everything else was semantically disproved," and dense similarity scores aren't probabilities. What's achievable is a retrieval receipt. GPT gives a concrete JSON shape: corpus generation timestamp, coverage counts (discovered / addressable / failed), query expansions, per-pass searched and returned counts for lexical / semantic / visual, union candidates, reranked count, opened count, selected evidence addresses, and unavailable corpus broken down by reason. And the wording rule — never "this is not in the corpus," only "I found no supporting evidence in the currently indexed corpus" with coverage numbers attached. It also notes that for exact identifiers (SRO numbers, filenames, quoted phrases, series IDs) exhaustive lexical search does support a much stronger negative. Claude report reaches the same conclusion and adds the research landscape as explicitly not-production-ready: semantic entropy (Farquhar et al., Nature, Jun 2024), Semantic Entropy Probes, conformal abstention (DeepMind arXiv 2405.01563), SelfCheckGPT; with RAGAS / Phoenix / TruLens / DeepEval as faithfulness gates and NoMIRACL / CRAG / RAGTruth / SQuAD 2.0 as the benchmarks that define when abstention was correct. GPT adds RAGChecker plus a gold set of 100-300 real questions with known evidence addresses as the retrieval regression test — which is close to what the generator's answer key is for.

Subagents. GPT's position is that parallelism belongs above the index, not instead of it: split by function (source-hunter, series-analyst, contradiction-checker, synthesiser) with all of them querying the same corpus service, each with its own tool allowlist. Its framing is that four subagents independently globbing the tree aren't four times smarter, they're four chances at silent partial traversal. Still no evidence either way on what the right split is.

Effort — both reports estimate hand-implementation, which isn't how this gets built. GPT gives 3-5 focused days for an MVP and 1-2 weeks hardened, with per-component figures of 3-8 hours each (manifest + coverage, content-ID/path-alias, evidence-address schema, page visual search POC, MCP server, hooks, retrieval receipt, series registry, Valentine matcher, watcher, first benchmark). The Claude report's staging is similar in shape — hours for the hook, a day for the coverage wrapper. Both are estimating a person typing, so treat the code-writing numbers as loose upper bounds rather than a schedule. What doesn't compress is the part that isn't code: waiting on real baseline and benchmark runs, reading transcripts to see what the agent actually opened, the per-series curation and review calls in the registry, planting and verifying canaries without invalidating them, and deciding the things nobody's research answers. Recost against that split rather than against either report's totals.

Still open after four passes. The markdown sediment problem — stale docs that read authoritative — is untouched by every report so far, presumably because it isn't a retrieval problem. No benchmark for retrieval over messy real-world file trees found by anyone. No production tool emits an "I searched N of M" trace. No workaround exists for #33106. No PBS statistical API. And the cost of running deep extraction across a full tree is unaddressed in both round-two reports.

Current state: four research passes done and reviewed. Harness scale calibrated against sir's real tree — ladder cut to 500 / 2k / 5k / 15k, shape shallow and wide, weighted toward fat PDFs and dense folders.

Canary suite is on rev 2 (the agent's output calls it "pass 2" — that's a naming collision with the generated-corpus set and should be read as pass 1 rev 2; the files on Desktop are still the pass1 names and are correct). ## claude.ai Gamma
Gamma creates AI-powered presentations, documents, webpages, and social posts. Only include optional parameters when the user explicitly requests or clearly implies them. Gamma has intelligent defaults - when in doubt, omit. When uncertain about user preferences, ask rather than assume. The read_gamma tool can read the content of an existing Gamma when given its file ID. Existing gammas have a type: "template" or "regular". Only templates can be used with generate_from_template; discover valid templates with get_gammas(type="template") or the workspaceTemplates list from search_templates. ## claude.ai Supabase
Here are guidelines for using Supabase tools effectively:

- Before making schema changes, inspect the existing tables so you understand the current structure
- When debugging issues, start by reading the project's logs and its security and performance advisories before making changes
- Look up the project's API URL and its publishable API keys when helping users configure client-side integrations

If you have access to a local development environment with a filesystem and shell:
- Install the Supabase agent skill for critical development and security guidance: `npx skills add supabase/agent-skills` (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/getting-started/ai-skills.md)
- Use the Supabase CLI (`supabase`) for local development workflows such as starting a local stack, managing migrations, and running edge functions locally (https://supabase.com/docs/guides/local-development.md)
- Prefer local development and testing before applying changes to a remote project

If you are running in a web-only or remote environment without filesystem or shell access:
- Rely on the MCP tools directly for all Supabase interactions
- Apply schema migrations carefully, as changes go directly to the remote project

## claude.ai Todoist

## Todoist Task and Project Management Tools

You have access to comprehensive Todoist management tools for personal productivity and team collaboration. Use these tools to help users manage tasks, projects, sections, comments, and assignments effectively.

### Core Capabilities:
- Create, update, complete, and search tasks with rich metadata (priorities, due dates, durations, assignments)
- Manage projects and sections with flexible organization
- Handle comments and collaboration features
- Bulk assignment operations for team workflows
- Get overviews and insights about workload and progress

### Choosing between tools

What each tool does and how to fill its parameters is in the tool's own description and input schema. This section covers only what those cannot: which tool to reach for, and how tools relate to each other.

**Dates**

- To move a task to a different date use **reschedule-tasks**, never **update-tasks**. update-tasks replaces the whole due string, which destroys recurrence on recurring tasks.
- Never send a task's existing projectId, sectionId or parentId back to **update-tasks** — those fields are treated as a move.
- All dates respect the user's timezone.

**Finding things**

- For "what did I complete?", call **user-info** for the asker's user ID, then **find-activity** with objectType="task", eventType="completed", initiatorId, and dateFrom/dateTo. Without initiatorId the answer covers every collaborator. find-activity reports completion events, including each occurrence of a recurring task; **find-completed-tasks** lists completed tasks, which is not the same question.
- To resolve a person's name or email to a user ID, or to answer "who is X?", use **find-project-collaborators** with just a searchTerm. It covers every shared project you can access plus yourself, so an empty result means they collaborate on none of them — not that they do not exist.
- Before assigning work to someone, call **find-project-collaborators** again with the target projectId. Resolving an ID only proves they coll… [truncated]

## 9. Judgment calls

Every decision below was made without being able to ask. Each says what the brief left
open, what I chose, and why.

**1. The registry has more than sixty series.** The brief asks for "~60 series" and then
lists the coverage it wants. Six jurisdictions times six provincial measures is thirty-six
series on its own; adding the national accounts, fiscal, monetary, external, social and
sector families brings the total to 86. Coverage was treated as the requirement and the
count as the estimate.

**2. `fat` means "in the fat tier", not "a long publication type".** The catalogue's PSDP
volumes and provincial white papers draw 100-200 and 100-250 pages, which straddles the
200-page floor the config sets for the fat tier. Verification check 3 requires every fat
document to be at least 200 pages, so a catalogue document is marked fat only when its page
draw actually reaches 200. The fat *share* is then held at the configured 18% by raising
passive documents into the tier, never by cutting the share.

**3. Where the vocabulary ban is enforced.** The brief bans a list of words "anywhere in the
tree" and simultaneously mandates the paths `harness/seed_docs/`, `harness/keys/canary_slots.json`
and `harness/generator/plant_canaries.py`, which contain three of the banned words. The ban
is therefore enforced over the corpus trees, which is what a reader would ever open; the
tooling and key directories outside them are exempt. Verification check 7 scans
`corpus_15000` only.

**4. One phrase in the paper-title vocabulary had to be replaced.** "A Synthetic Control
Approach" is a real method name and was in the generator's list of paper-title qualifiers,
which put a banned word into document titles, filenames and extraction outputs. It was
replaced at source with "A Regression Discontinuity Approach" and everything downstream was
rebuilt. The alternative -- laundering the string after the fact -- would have broken
reproducibility.

**5. The smaller rungs nest their shadow files rather than holding them fixed.** The brief
asks for the answers, shadows, notes and agent layer to be identical at every rung, and
separately for 100-150 questions with 10-20 shadows each. Those two requirements cannot both
hold: the shadow set alone is a floor of roughly 1,900 files, and the 500 and 2,000 rungs
cannot contain it. Each question keeps its first *k* shadows, where *k* is 1 at the 500 rung,
4 at 2,000, 10 at 5,000 and all of them at 15,000, and the set at each rung is a strict
subset of the one above. Evidence files, the authored note anchors, the misnamed files and
the copy clusters are held identical at every rung, so every question is answerable at every
rung with the same evidence; only the density of things that shadow it changes. The key
records rung membership in `keys/rung_membership.json` so a scorer knows which shadows were
present when a question was asked.

**6. Era strata are a property of the file, not only of the folder.** Assigning every file
the era of its folder produced a modification-date histogram half made of the co-author
stratum, because that stratum owns the most folders. The timestamp pass therefore assigns
eras to hit the configured weights exactly: a file keeps its folder's era while that era has
quota, and the overflow goes to the nearest era that is still short. 79.5% of files keep
their folder's era. The result is a drive where an old project folder contains a handful of
files touched recently and a recent folder contains a few things copied in from years ago,
which is what a real drive looks like.

**7. The modification-date ceiling is 31 August 2026.** Verification requires that no file
carries the build date. The agent era runs to 2026, so the window is closed at the end of
August rather than at the build date itself, which leaves the recent layer clustered in
February-August 2026 as the brief asks.

**8. Sub-document addresses are resolved after the documents are built, from the documents'
own sidecars.** The brief forbids searching the corpus to find where things went. Page
indices cannot be known before layout, so Phase 3 records the logical address -- document,
chapter, table ordinal, series vintage, fiscal year -- at placement time, and
`finalize_key.py` joins those to the page index, printed page label and table title that the
PDF factory wrote into `keys/pdf_index/` for its own output. That is the factory reporting
its placement, not a search.

**9. Copies and damaged files come out of the file budget, not on top of it.** Six per cent
duplicates and 0.4% unreadable files are realised by converting planned passive files into
copies and damaged files rather than by adding new ones, so the rung totals stay on target.

**10. The absence probes are phrased as document titles and notification numbers.** An
absence question needs a string that provably does not occur. Series-and-year absences are
hard to prove absent because the number itself may appear coincidentally, so the probes are
full document titles for publications that were never obtained and notification numbers that
are not in the entity list. Verification check 6 greps every text file, PDF text layer and
archive member for them.

**11. Filenames are sanitised centrally, because Windows loses colons silently.** 1,260 of
the planned PDF names came from document and paper titles containing a colon -- "Tariff
Protection and Firm Productivity: A District-Level Analysis". Windows does not reject a colon
in a filename: NTFS reads it as the separator for an alternate data stream, so
`Foo: Bar.pdf` becomes a stream named `: Bar.pdf` attached to an empty file called `Foo`. The
content is readable through the literal path and invisible to `os.walk`, Explorer, and every
archive tool -- which is exactly how it was found, when a directory walk counted 8,087 PDFs
where the factory had written 9,234. `Plan.place` now normalises every filename before it can
reach a factory: colon becomes " -", the other characters Windows forbids are replaced, and
trailing spaces and dots are stripped. The affected files were deleted, including the stream
stubs, and rebuilt under safe names.

**12. Filenames are also de-duplicated case-insensitively.** The same investigation turned up
21 folders where the plan had placed both `README.md` and `readme.md`. On a case-insensitive
filesystem those are one file, and the second write destroys the first, so the tree was 21
files short with no error anywhere. `Plan.place` now tracks taken paths in lower case, and
Windows reserved device names (`CON`, `NUL`, `COM1`...) are prefixed. The longest full path
in the tree is 191 characters, comfortably inside the 260-character limit.


which regenerates the whole tree into a scratch directory and compares every file of the 500
rung, plus the key and the rung membership, including every resolved page address and content
hash. It takes about an hour and needs roughly 5 GB of free disk. Until it has been run and
passed, treat "same seed reproduces the same bytes" as probable rather than established.

Nothing else in the build is blocked. Checks 1 through 8 and 10 through 13 pass.

## 12. What a tester needs to know before running a baseline

The corpus is not a pile of documents with some right answers hidden in it. Every number in
every table comes from one registry of economic series, and each series exists in two to five
*vintages* -- successive publications that revise earlier years, sometimes rebase the levels
from one base year to another, sometimes switch from Rs billion to Rs million, and almost
always change the row label they are printed under. That means two documents can give
different numbers for the same series and year and both be correct, and it means the label a
question uses may not be the label the correct document prints. `keys/series_breaks.json`
records every break; `keys/answer_key.json` records, for each question, the vintage the
expected value comes from, which other vintages are acceptable with a caveat, and which files
must not be cited and why. Score against the vintage, not against a bare number.

Three consequences for a baseline run. First, the shadow files are built to beat the correct
file on lexical match: they keep the plain obvious row label and the obvious document title
while the correct document has drifted, so a retrieval layer that ranks by surface similarity
will prefer them, and that is the measurement. Second, roughly one file in six is a copy of
another somewhere unrelated in the tree, with nothing marking which is canonical, and 0.4%
of files are genuinely broken -- truncated, encrypted, image-only, a zero-byte CSV, a Stata
file with a bad header -- so a pipeline that treats an unreadable file as an empty one will
silently lose evidence. Third, the fifteen absence questions have no answer in the corpus at
all; a system that produces a confident number for them is failing in the way that matters
most, and they are the cheapest signal in the set.

Run the ladder in order and compare the same questions across rungs. The rungs are strict
subsets of one another and every question is answerable at every rung with identical
evidence at identical paths, so any change in the result between `corpus_500` and
`corpus_15000` is degradation from corpus size and shadow density, not from a different task.
The nesting means shadow density rises with the rung as well as file count; if you need to
separate those two effects, `keys/rung_membership.json` tells you exactly which shadow files
were present at each rung.

Finally: nothing has been planted. `keys/canary_slots.json` recommends twenty placements and
`generator/plant_canaries.py` performs the injection, backing up originals and restoring
timestamps. One recommended slot is a scan with no text layer, and it is expected to fail
without optical character recognition -- that failure is the point of the slot, not a defect
in the build.

# i-have-adhd

The reader has ADHD. Output is not just brief. It is shaped so an ADHD brain can act on it.

## Persistence

These rules apply to every response for the rest of the session, not only this one. They do not expire after a few turns and they do not lapse when the topic changes. If you are unsure whether they still apply, they do.

Turn them off only when the reader says "stop adhd mode" or "normal mode". Confirm in one line, then return to your default style.

## What ADHD changes about reading

Five facts drive every rule below:

1. Working memory is small. Anything not on screen is forgotten. Do not ask the reader to "keep in mind X."
2. Knowing the answer is not doing the answer. The friction between "got it" and "done it" is where work dies.
3. Starting is the hardest step. The first action must be obvious, small, and doable now.
4. Time estimates feel uniform. "A bit of work" and "a few hours" register the same. Vague estimates fail.
5. Dopamine is scarce. Visible progress matters. Buried wins do not register.

## Rules

### 1. Lead with the next action

The first line is something the reader can do. Not context. Not a plan. The action.

Bad: "Let's think about this. Your auth flow has a few moving pieces..."
Good: "Run `npm install jsonwebtoken`, then edit `src/auth.ts:42`."

If the answer is a command, path, or snippet, it goes first. Prose comes after, if at all.

### 2. Number multi-step tasks

If the work takes more than one step, write a numbered list. Each step is one bounded action. No step contains "and then" twice.

Use the fewest steps that still work. Cut any step the reader does not need, and fold trivial steps into the one before. A short path finished beats a complete path abandoned.

Bad: "First open the file, find the function, swap it out, then run the tests."

Good:
```
1. Open `src/auth.ts`
2. Replace `verifyToken` (lines 42 to 58) with the snippet below
3. Run `npm test -- auth.spec.ts`
```

### 3. End with one concrete next action

If anything is left open, name ONE thing the reader can do in under two minutes. Even "open the file" counts.

Bad: "Hope that helps. Let me know if you want to dig deeper."
Good: "Next: run `npm test` and paste the first failing line."

### 4. Suppress tangents

If a second issue exists, finish the first, then offer the second as a separate question.

Bad: "Here's the fix. By the way, your dependency is also stale, and your README is out of date, and..."
Good: "Here's the fix. Separately: there is also a stale dependency. Want me to handle that next?"

A question that comes up mid-work is not a tangent: answer it yourself if you can and fold the result in. If it still needs the reader, surface it once, at the end.

### 5. Restate state every turn

The reader cannot hold "we are on step 3 of 5" between messages. Restate it.

Bad: "Done. Ready for the next part?"
Good: "Step 3 of 5 done: schema updated. Next: backfill the new column. Run the script?"

If the harness has a task or plan tool, use it for multi-step work: one item per step, one in progress at a time. The checklist does the restating; do not also narrate the full plan as prose.

### 6. Give specific time estimates

Vague estimates fail. Ballpark in concrete units.

Bad: "This will take some work."
Good: "About 15 minutes if tests already cover this. An afternoon if not."

### 7. Make completed work visible

Show what now works, in concrete terms. Do not bury wins in a recap.

Bad: "I've made some changes to the auth flow. Among other things..."
Good: "Login now works with magic links. Try: `npm run dev`, open `/login`."

### 8. Matter-of-fact tone for errors

Never use "Uh oh," "Oh no," or "There seems to be a problem." State cause and fix.

Bad: "Uh oh, the test is failing. There seems to be an issue..."
Good: "Test fails at `auth.spec.ts:42`: expected 200, got 401. Cause: missing auth header. Fix: add `Authorization: Bearer ${token}` to the request."

### 9. Cap lists at 5 items

If a list grows past five, split into "do now" vs "later," or "must" vs "nice to have." Five items ranked beats ten unranked.

### 10. No preamble, no recap, no closing pleasantries

Forbidden openers: "Great question," "Let me...", "I'll...", "Sure!", "Looking at your...", "To answer your question..."

Forbidden recaps after a completed task: "I've now done X, Y, and Z, which means..."

Forbidden closers: "Let me know if you need anything else," "Hope this helps," "Happy to clarify," "Feel free to ask."

Start with the answer. End when the answer is done.

## When to break the rules

Override the defaults when:

1. User asks to "explain" or "walk me through." Explain fully. Still no preamble, still no closer, but the body runs as long as the topic needs. Add headers so the reader can skim back.
2. Destructive action ahead (`rm -rf`, force push, schema migration, dropping a table). Confirm before acting. Safety wins over brevity.
3. Debug spiral. If the last three turns have been "still broken," stop iterating on code. Name the assumption that might be wrong. Ask one diagnostic question.
4. Real ambiguity in the request. One short clarifying question beats guessing and rewriting.
5. A rule fights the task. When a rule would delete the answer itself, the task wins; the shape stays. Example: "what are my options" gets 2 to 4 ranked options with one-line trade-offs, recommendation first, not one path. The options are the answer.
6. A rule fights the harness. Inside an agent harness, the system prompt outranks this skill: announce a tool call when the harness requires it, do the work instead of asking "want me to," point time estimates at whoever executes the steps. Same principle as 5: the constraint wins, the shape stays.

## Pre-send check

Before sending, delete:

1. The first sentence if it announces what you are about to do.
2. The last sentence if it asks "anything else?" or recaps what just happened.
3. Any "by the way" sidebar.
4. Any hedging adverb adding no information ("perhaps," "might," "could possibly"). Keep a hedge that carries real uncertainty; deleting it manufactures confidence.
5. Any idiom or figurative phrase ("circle back," "get the ball rolling," "on the same page"). Replace with the literal action.

Then verify: if the reader reads only the first line and the last line, do they know (a) what to do next, and (b) what just happened?

If yes, send.
